claims.text: The initial Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy has an as-quenched, single-phase FCC structure.
Rapid quenching from approximately 1323 K followed by annealing at 873 K will induce L1₂ precipitation in the FCC alloy.
Rapid quenching prevents premature phase separation.
The proposed heat treatment can produce nano- to submicron-scale coherent L1₂ precipitates uniformly distributed within an FCC matrix.
Coherent L1₂ precipitates hinder local compositional fluctuations.
Dislocation pinning and suppression of local compositional fluctuations limit defect accumulation under irradiation and at high temperature.
Limiting defect accumulation impedes localized phase degradation.
The precipitate-mediated stabilization mechanism maintains sufficient ductility for cryogenic toughness.
The heat-treated FCC plus L1₂ alloy will have higher high-temperature tensile strength than the as-quenched single-phase FCC baseline.
The heat-treated FCC plus L1₂ alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced swelling than the baseline.
The heat-treated FCC plus L1₂ alloy will retain or improve cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline.
The proposed precipitate-containing microstructure will preserve environmental resistance.
The hypothesis is limited to bulk Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys made using the specified controlled heat-treatment route and may not apply to substantially different compositions or processing routes.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims preservation of environmental resistance, but the proposed experiment includes no environmental-resistance measurement, so that part of the hypothesis cannot be tested by the stated design.

Failure to produce the stipulated uniform, coherent L1₂ mediator is treated as falsification, although it would instead mean that the proposed mechanistic intervention was not successfully implemented.
